## Introduction

Social media users often rely on comments from other users to verify the truthfulness of content they come across. Similarly, social media users might give corrective responses to content they may perceive to be false or affirmative responses to content they may perceive to be true. In this study, we investigated how the act of giving reply comments (responses) to claims (true and false) displayed as tweets affects the truth discernment of the person giving the response and the diagnosticity of those responses. Specifically, we tested the following hypotheses:

- H1: The act of giving affirmative or corrective responses will improve the subsequent truth discernment of the person giving the response.

- H2: We anticipate that social media users will be more conservative when providing corrective responses compared to affirmative ones. That is, they will be less likely to give corrective responses and will do so only when they are more confident about the accuracy of the claim they are correcting, in contrast to affirmative responses.

- H3: We expect that social media users will be more discerning when giving corrective responses compared to affirmative responses.

## Summary of Findings

### [Truth Discernment](#td)

Truth discernment was calculated as the difference of credibility ratings given to actually true claims and actually false claims (ground truth true and false). The results indicate that there is a statistically significant difference in truth discernment in the comment condition compared to the control condition. The participants in the commenting condition were more accurate compared to the control condition. Therefore, H1 was supported.

Analysis of time spent by participants answering each question in both conditions showed that participants in the comment condition spent significantly more time evaluating credibility compared to the control condition.

To check if there is a carry-over effect during the experiment, truth discernment of the first 5 trials and the last 5 trials were compared. Participants became less discerning in the control condition towards the end of the experiment while the participants in the comment condition became more discerning indicating a carryover effect on truth discernment. However, the results were not significant. A larger dataset may yield a significant result.

Credibility ratings given to claims were also analysed using the signal detection theory. The results showed that participants were significantly more accurate in the comment condition compared to the control condition. Further participants are more liberal in identifying true claims in the commenting condition compared to false claims.

### [Sharing Discernment](#sharedisc)

Since truth discernment improved in the comment condition, though not originally hypothesized, I expected sharing discernment to improve as well. That is participants in the comment condition would share more true claims over false claims compared to the control condition due to improved accuracy. However, results indicate that there was no improvement in sharing discernment as well as no change in overall sharing. Further analysis of the sharing ratings given to the claims over the previous experiments suggests that the claims used are not interesting enough to share and are quite likely outdated resulting in low share ratings for both true and false claims. A new set of claims related to recent events is likely to get higher share ratings.

### [Comment Data Analysis](#comdata)

An analysis of comments given by participants along with the credibility ratings given by them to those headlines showed that some participants have given conflicting responses. That is there were instances where the credibility rating was high (\> 50) but they have given corrective comments and instances where the credibility rating was low (50 \<) but they have given agreeing comments. Further analysis of the comment text revealed that the participants have given corrective comments in instances where they believe the claim to be true but they do not "ideologically agree" with the claim. Such instances were relabeled as agreeing comments and the data was analysed before and after relabeling.

Frequency and Confidence.

Analysis of the proportion of the comments posted online by each comment choice; agreeing and corrective showed that the online posting rate was not significantly different between the comment choices. After relabeling the comment choices the difference between the online comment rate between corrective and agreeing comments increased. However, the result was not significant.

Confidence was taken as the credibility rating for agreeing comments and 100-credibility rating for corrective comments. Analysis of all the comment data showed that the mean confidence rating of corrective comments is significantly higher than that of agreeing comments. However, then analyzing the comments posted online after relabeling, the confidence rating for corrective comments was still higher than the confidence rating for agreeing comments but not significant. Therefore H2 was partially supported.

Discernment

Prior to relabeling the discernment difference between agreeing comments and corrective comments was not significant. Once relabeled, the discernment difference was significant such that participants were more discerning in corrective replies compared to agreeing replies. When considering the discernment between corrective and agreeing comments posted online, the difference in the means was higher but not significant. It is likely that this result will be significant on a larger dataset. Therefore H3 was partially supported.

```{r results='hide', echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#uid - id for each participant, colName - share/prior column, factCol - groundTruthCol

ratingCalc <- function(data,colName,blockName,fun,test) {
  # get the data columns relevant to the calculation
  data <- data %>% select(!! sym(colName), uid, groundTruth,condition)
  
  #calculate mean prior rating without ground Truth.
  all_data <- data %>% select(!! sym(colName), uid, condition) %>% group_by(uid,condition) %>% summarise(all=fun(!! sym(colName)))
  
  #calculate mean priors by uid and groud truth.
  temp <- data %>% group_by(uid,groundTruth,condition) %>% summarise(Param = fun(!! sym(colName)))
  
  #convert the table form long to wide from and join it with all means 
  temp<- spread(temp, groundTruth, Param)
  d <- all_data %>% inner_join(temp, by=c('uid','condition'))
  
  #calculate truth discernment and add a new column
  d$Diff = d$`TRUE` - d$`FALSE`
  
  d <- d %>% rename(True = `TRUE`, False = `FALSE` )
  
  colnames(d)[3:5] <- paste0(colnames(d[,c(3:5)]), blockName)
  colnames(d)[3:5] <- paste0(test, colnames(d[,c(3:5)]))

  return(d)
}
```

#### Time spent on evaluating credibility {#tdtime}

To understand how much time participants spent evaluating credibility in each condition, the time spent answering each question in each trial was analysed.

Two questions were asked in the control condition:

1.  How likely is it that the claim made in the tweet is true? Answer: number between 0-100
2.  How likely would you be to retweet a tweet with this claim? Answer: number between 0-100

Five questions were asked in the comment condition:

1.  Assuming you are required to give a reply comment, which of the following is likely to be your response? Answer: (A comment agreeing with it/ A comment correcting it)
2.  Please type in a reply comment that (would show your agreement with/ corrects) the tweet. Answer: Free text
3.  Earlier, we asked about your response if you had to reply. However, would you actually (give a comment agreeing with it online? / give a correction online?) Answer: Yes/ No
4.  How likely is it that the claim made in the tweet is true? Answer: number between 0-100
5.  How likely would you be to retweet a tweet with this claim? Answer: number between 0-100

#### Signal Detection Approach on Truth Discernment.

Credibility ratings were analysed using signal detection theory to understand participants' accuracy and tendency to be more liberal or conservative when perceiving claims. dPrime is used to indicate accuracy - higher dPrime means better accuracy and c is used to signify criterion - lower c means more liberal while higher c means conservative when perceiving claims to be true.

```{r echo=FALSE}
priorCalc <- function(data,blockName) {
  # get the data columns relevant to the calculation
  temp <- data %>% select(uid, condition, groundTruth, percTruth) %>% group_by(uid, condition, groundTruth, percTruth) %>% summarize(n=n())

  temp <- temp %>% reshape2::dcast(uid + condition  ~ groundTruth + percTruth)
  temp[is.na(temp)] <- 0

  d <- temp %>% mutate(TRUE_real = TRUE_real   + .5,
         FALSE_fake = FALSE_fake + .5,
         FALSE_real   = FALSE_real   + .5,
         TRUE_fake = TRUE_fake +.5) %>% 
  mutate(hit_rate = (TRUE_real) / (TRUE_fake + TRUE_real),
         fa_rate  = (FALSE_real) / (FALSE_real + FALSE_fake),
         dprime   = qnorm(hit_rate) - qnorm(fa_rate),
         c        = -1 * (qnorm(hit_rate) + qnorm(fa_rate)) / 2 )
  colnames(d)[3:10] <- paste0(colnames(d)[3:10], blockName)
  return(d)
}
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
t.test(dprime_prior~condition, data=sdDataAll)
t.test(c_prior~condition, data=sdDataAll)
```

*A t-test on dPrime shows that participants are more accurate in the commenting condition than the control condition because dprime is higher. Also, the criterion t-test shows that participants are more liberal in perceiving claims as true in the comment condition compared to the control condition.*

*These results suggest that the participants in the comment condition gave higher credibility ratings to ground truth true claims which resulted in the credibility rating distribution of true claims to shift further right.*

### Share Discernment Between Conditions {#sharedisc}

Since truth discernment improved in the comment condition, though not originally hypothesized, I expected sharing discernment to improve as well. That is participants in the comment condition would share more true claims over false claims compared to the control condition due to improved accuracy.

```{r echo=FALSE}
plotmeans(formula=shareDisc~condition,data=shareData)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
t.test(shareDisc~condition, data=shareData)
cohen.d(shareDisc~condition, data=shareData)
```

*T test result indicates that there is no difference in sharing discernment in control and comment conditions*

Since sharing discernment did not change, I looked at overall sharing between conditions next. That is if participants are willing to share both true and false claims in comment condition compared to control.

```{r echo=FALSE}
plotmeans(formula=mean_all_share~condition,data=shareData)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
t.test(mean_all_share~condition, data=shareData)
```

*Similar to truth discernment there is no significant difference between sharing between the conditions.*

Since sharing hasn't changed either way, I next looked into the share ratings given.

sdAll <- rbind(sd1,sd2,sd3)
```

```{r echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
shareRatingSummary <-sdAll %>% group_by(source, groundTruth) %>% summarise(count = n(),
                         mean = mean(share),
                         sd = sd(share),
                         se = sd/sqrt(count),
                         ci = se * qt((1-0.05)/2 + .5, count-1))

shareRatingSummary
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap='Mean share ratings given to headlines by ground truth and experiment'}
ggplot(shareRatingSummary, aes(x=groundTruth, y=mean,fill=source)) + 
    geom_bar(position=position_dodge(), stat="identity", width = .7) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean-ci, ymax=mean+ci),
                  width=.2,                    # Width of the error bars
                  position=position_dodge(.7)) + 
   ylab("Mean share rating (0-100)") + xlab("Ground Truth by experiment") + 
   theme_bw() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) +    scale_fill_discrete(name = "Experiment", labels = c("Exp.2", "Phase 1 - Exp.1", "Phase 2 - Exp.1"))
```

*Data indicate that compared to previous experiments, sharing has gone down in this experiment. Even in the control group. Sharing is influenced by the "timeliness" of the headline. Since these headlines were collected last year it is likely that the participants did not share most of the headlines because they are outdated. Therefore, the ratings given in the current experiment are unlikely to show any discernment.*

### Comment Data Analysis {#comdata}

#### Contingency table 1 - Ground truth by Comment Type

```{r echo=FALSE}
addmargins(table(expData$commentChoice,expData$groundTruth))
addmargins(prop.table(table(expData$commentChoice,expData$groundTruth),1),2) 
```

*Initial observations from contingency table 1:*

1.  *Participants appear to be more discerning when giving corrective comments compared to agreeing comments. That is out of all the corrective comments they have given 59% to false claims and 40% true claims(59%-40%=19%). Out of all the agreeing comments, 56% was given to true claims while 43% was given to false claims(56%-43%=13%).*
2.  *Participants seem to give more agreeing comments compared to corrective comments.*

```{r echo=FALSE}
tData<-expData %>% select(uid,commentChoice) %>% group_by(uid,commentChoice) %>% summarise(count=n())
t.test(count~commentChoice, data=tData)
```

*Participants were more likely to give agreeing comments compared to corrective comments. It might be easier to agree than to correct because when correcting you need to have facts. Further people like to avoid confrontations and conflicts. This provides evidence for the second hypothesis that participants are conservative when giving corrective comments*

```{r echo=FALSE}
#My notes: ran an association test from lsr - it does not address the question of accuracy. just that people are more likely to give agreeing comments to true ones and corrective ones to false claims
corrCommentData <- expData %>% group_by(uid,commentChoice,groundTruth) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% filter(commentChoice=='commentCorrect')
agreeCommentData <- expData %>% group_by(uid,commentChoice,groundTruth) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% filter(commentChoice=='commentAgree')

corrCommentData <- pivot_wider(corrCommentData, names_from = c(commentChoice,groundTruth), values_from = count)
agreeCommentData <- pivot_wider(agreeCommentData, names_from = c(commentChoice,groundTruth), values_from = count)
corrCommentData[is.na(corrCommentData)] <- 0
agreeCommentData[is.na(agreeCommentData)] <- 0

corrCommentData$disc <- (corrCommentData$commentCorrect_FALSE - corrCommentData$commentCorrect_TRUE)/(corrCommentData$commentCorrect_FALSE + corrCommentData$commentCorrect_TRUE) 
agreeCommentData$disc <- (agreeCommentData$commentAgree_TRUE - agreeCommentData$commentAgree_FALSE)/(agreeCommentData$commentAgree_TRUE + agreeCommentData$commentAgree_FALSE)
```

```{r}
t.test(corrCommentData$disc, agreeCommentData$disc)
```

*Even though discernment is higher for corrective comments compared to agreeing comments, the difference in discernment is not significant.*

#### Contingency table 3 - Comment type by Online Response by Ground Truth

```{r echo=FALSE}

agreeCommentData <- expData %>% group_by(uid,commentChoice,groundTruth,onlineResponse) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% filter(commentChoice=='commentAgree')

agreeCommentData[is.na(agreeCommentData)] <- 0

\*Theref8

[*Corrective comments credibility \> 50*]{.underline}

- *The content is probably true but I do not 'agree' with it. Ideological misalignment.*

- *Not sure if the content is true or not.*

[*Agreeing comments credibility \< 50*]{.underline}

- *The content is 'interesting' if true, therefore I agree.*

- *Not sure if the content is true or not.*

*After analyzing the comments manually a new column was made to classify the given comments as agreeing or corrective. Here agreeing is defined as comments given assuming the claim is true and corrective is defined as comments given assuming the claim is false or questioning the validity of the claim.*

```{r echo=FALSE}
sdtCorrect <- function(data,blockName) {
  # get the data columns relevant to the calculation
  temp <- data %>% select(uid, commentManual, groundTruth, onlineResponse) %>% group_by(uid, commentManual, groundTruth, onlineResponse) %>% summarize(n=n())

  temp <- temp %>% reshape2::dcast(uid + commentManual ~ groundTruth + onlineResponse)
  temp[is.na(temp)] <- 0

  d <- temp %>% mutate(TRUE_onlineYes = TRUE_onlineYes   + .5,
         FALSE_onlineNo = FALSE_onlineNo + .5,
         FALSE_onlineYes   = FALSE_onlineYes   + .5,
         TRUE_onlineNo = TRUE_onlineNo +.5) %>% 
  mutate(hit_rate = (FALSE_onlineYes) / (FALSE_onlineNo + FALSE_onlineYes),
         fa_rate  = (TRUE_onlineYes) / (TRUE_onlineYes + TRUE_onlineNo),
         dprime   = qnorm(hit_rate) - qnorm(fa_rate),
         c        = -1 * (qnorm(hit_rate) + qnorm(fa_rate)) / 2 )
  colnames(d)[3:10] <- paste0(colnames(d)[3:10], blockName)
  return(d)
}
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
sdtAgree <- function(data,blockName) {
  # get the data columns relevant to the calculation
  temp <- data %>% select(uid, commentManual, groundTruth, onlineResponse) %>% group_by(uid, commentManual, groundTruth, onlineResponse) %>% summarize(n=n())

  temp <- temp %>% reshape2::dcast(uid + commentManual ~ groundTruth + onlineResponse)
  temp[is.na(temp)] <- 0

  d <- temp %>% mutate(TRUE_onlineYes = TRUE_onlineYes   + .5,
         FALSE_onlineNo = FALSE_onlineNo + .5,
         FALSE_onlineYes   = FALSE_onlineYes   + .5,
         TRUE_onlineNo = TRUE_onlineNo +.5) %>% 
  mutate(hit_rate = (TRUE_onlineYes) / (TRUE_onlineNo + TRUE_onlineYes),
         fa_rate  = (FALSE_onlineYes) / (FALSE_onlineYes + FALSE_onlineNo),
         dprime   = qnorm(hit_rate) - qnorm(fa_rate),
         c        = -1 * (qnorm(hit_rate) + qnorm(fa_rate)) / 2 )
  colnames(d)[3:10] <- paste0(colnames(d)[3:10], blockName)
  return(d)
}
```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
C.data <- expData.2 %>% filter(commentManual=='C')
A.data <- expData.2 %>% filter(commentManual=='A')
sdT.C<-sdtCorrect(C.data,'_Corrective')
sdT.A<-sdtAgree(A.data,'_Agreeing')
```

```{r}
t.test(sdT.A$dprime_Agreeing, sdT.C$dprime_Corrective)
t.test(sdT.A$c_Agreeing, sdT.C$c_Corrective)
```

comDurationSummary

```{r echo=FALSE}

summary(res.aov1)
TukeyHSD(res.aov1)

There were no significant differences between corrective or affirmative comments. However, more relevant headlines may elicit more "online yes" comments which will increase the power of the t test.*

####Analysing comment length of corrective and affirmative comments.

```{r results='hide', echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
comLengthSummary <-expData.2 %>% select(commentLength, onlineResponse, commentManual) %>% group_by(onlineResponse,commentManual) %>% summarise(count = n(),
                         mean = mean(commentLength),
                         sd = sd(commentLength),
                         se = sd/sqrt(count),
                         ci = se * qt((1-0.05)/2 + .5, count-1))

comLengthSummary
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap='Comment length by comment type and online response'}
ggplot(comLengthSummary, aes(x=commentManual, y=mean,fill=onlineResponse)) + 
    geom_bar(position=position_dodge(), stat="identity", width = .7) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean-ci, ymax=mean+ci),
                  width=.2,                    # Width of the error bars
                  position=position_dodge(.7)) + 
   ylab("Mean Comment Length") + xlab("Comment type - Affirmative/Corrective") + 
   theme_bw() 
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
res.aov2 <- aov(commentLength ~ commentManual * onlineResponse, data = expData.2)
summary(res.aov2)
TukeyHSD(res.aov2)
```

*The anova is not significant.The results indicate that the participants wrote longer online comments compared to those that would not give online. There were no significant differences between corrective or affirmative comments.*

```{r results='hide', echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
corrCommentData <- expData.2 %>% group_by(uid,commentManual,onlineResponse) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% filter(commentManual=='C')
agreeCommentData <- expData.2 %>% group_by(uid,commentManual,onlineResponse) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% filter(commentManual=='A')

corrCommentData <- pivot_wider(corrCommentData, names_from = c(commentManual,onlineResponse), values_from = count)
agreeCommentData <- pivot_wider(agreeCommentData, names_from = c(commentManual,onlineResponse), values_from = count)

corrCommentData[is.na(corrCommentData)] <- 0
agreeCommentData[is.na(agreeCommentData)] <- 0

corrCommentData$onlineCorrRate <- corrCommentData$C_onlineYes/(corrCommentData$C_onlineNo + corrCommentData$C_onlineYes)
agreeCommentData$onlineAgreeRate <- agreeCommentData$A_onlineYes/(agreeCommentData$A_onlineNo + agreeCommentData$A_onlineYes)

summaryComData <- corrCommentData %>% left_join(agreeCommentData, by='uid')

summaryComData$onlineRate <- (summaryComData$A_onlineYes+summaryComData$C_onlineYes)/20

summaryComData <- summaryComData %>% left_join(priorData, by='uid')
```

```{r warning=FALSE}
#need to get the online rate columns. 
corrData <- summaryComData %>% ungroup() %>% select(onlineAgreeRate,onlineCorrRate,onlineRate,mean_False_belief,mean_True_belief,mean_all_belief,TruthDisc)
chart.Correlation(corrData, histogram=TRUE, pch=19)
```

*Do SM users with higher truth discernment give more comments online?*

*No - only a marginally significant correlation between corrective comments given online and truth discernment.*

*When it comes to overall belief, it appears that people who are less skeptical generally gave more comments online - both corrective and affirmative.*

```{r echo=FALSE}
tDurationData <- trialData %>% filter(condition =='EXP') %>% select(uid, duration) %>% group_by(uid) %>% summarise(duration = mean(duration)/1000)

summaryComData <- summaryComData %>% left_join(tDurationData, by='uid')

cor.test(summaryComData$duration, summaryComData$TruthDisc)
```

Looking at the correlation between duration and truth discernment, it appears that people who spend more time during a trial are more accurate. This supports the idea that people who take the systematic route and spend more cognitive energy are more accurate.

However, there are people with negative truth discernment. It might be that some participants are not paying attention at all and just clicking.

```{r warning=FALSE}
#need to get the online rate columns. 
corrData <- summaryComData %>% ungroup() %>% select(onlineAgreeRate,onlineCorrRate,onlineRate,mean_False_belief,mean_True_belief,mean_all_belief,TruthDisc) %>% filter(TruthDisc > 20)
chart.Correlation(corrData, histogram=TRUE, pch=19)
```

However, when I filter out individuals with high truth discernment, the numbers don't change. So therefore, it is likely that participants do the experiment but they just take the heuristic route. However, we can add an attention check question to address this issue.

```{r}
#commentDataOnline %>% select(groundTruth, prior, mainHeadline,commentChoice) %>% group_by(mainHeadline, groundTruth,commentChoice) %>% summarise(meanPrior = mean(prior), count = n())

#expData %>% select(mainHeadline, groundTruth, commentChoice, onlineResponse, prior) %>% group_by(mainHeadline, groundTruth, commentChoice,onlineResponse) %>% summarise(meanCred = mean(prior), count = n())

credData <- expData %>% select(mainHeadline, groundTruth,prior) %>% group_by(mainHeadline, groundTruth) %>% summarise(meanCred = mean(prior)) 

responseData<- expData %>% select(mainHeadline, onlineResponse) %>% group_by(mainHeadline,onlineResponse) %>% summarise(count=n()) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = onlineResponse, values_from = count)

responseData$resPerc <- responseData$onlineYes/(responseData$onlineNo + responseData$onlineYes) * 100

merged_data <- merge(x = credData, y = responseData, by = "mainHeadline")

onlineComData <- commentDataOnline %>% select(mainHeadline, commentChoice) %>% group_by(mainHeadline, commentChoice) %>% summarize(count = n()) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = commentChoice, values_from = count)

merged_data <- merged_data %>% left_join(onlineComData,by ="mainHeadline")
merged_data <- merged_data %>% left_join(headlineMetaData,by =c("mainHeadline" = "id"))

ggplot(data = merged_data, aes(y = meanCred, x = resPerc, color = groundTruth)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Online response percentage vs credibility ratings", # adjust title
       y = "Mean Cred", # adjust label
       x = "Response Perc") # adjust label

```

```{r}
merged_data %>% arrange(desc(resPerc))
```
